title: AI test as youth protest
full_text:
Tasmania’s AI plans are under fresh scrutiny as chief scientists from the biggest AI companies warn against unfettered growth worldwide, with the state’s youth vowing to ramp up pressure on politicians with further school strikes.
The chief scientists from OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta AI along with more than 1000 other AI employees signed a letter that requested the US government “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”.
The letter warned that the world lacks “the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress”.
The “AI frontier” workers said there was a real risk that capability development would accelerate beyond human ability to control or understand the resulting systems.
In a response to the Mercury, Tasmania’s Minister for Innovation, Science and the Digital Economy Felix Ellis reaffirmed the government’s support for “the increased adoption of AI across both government and the private sector”.
He said the government understood the need to progress AI in “a safe, responsible and ethical way” and said the government noted “ongoing work internationally to strengthen safeguards for advanced AI models and will continue to monitor developments”.
He said the state looked forward “to engaging in national processes to ensure Tasmania’s interests and priorities are reflected in the development of standards that benefit Tasmanians.” Mr Ellis said the government would be releasing “a draft Tasmanian Statement of Expectations for Data Centres and AI Infrastructure” for public consultation.
The letter comes after more than 100 school- and university-aged people protested against Tasmania’s AI development plans in Launceston on Wednesday.
Ellie Charlton, 21, from community group CIRCA Lutruwita said with one AI centre under construction and two others planned, the state was at the forefront of “sweeping unparalleled changes, data retention and mass invasion of privacy”.
Ms Charlton said the group would continue to strike until the Firmus projects were all cancelled, and the government was “absolutely not” listening to their concerns after the Premier responded to the protests that AI was “here to stay”.
Protesters on Wednesday spoke about the negative effect AI has on workers and students, AI usage at UTAS, and Firmus founder Oliver Curtis’s previous criminal convictions.
Ms Charlton said preserving mental integrity, child safety and the environment were a major concern for the group “in the age on anti-intellectualism, rampant child sexual abuse material and climate change”. It comes after the George Town Council rejected a petition with more than 5000 signatures that called on the council to reject the development application of the facility at Long Reach, over a technicality.
